awd_titl_txt: Doctoral Dissertation Research: Understanding of Trade and Diplomatic Relations
awd_abstract_narration:
This doctoral dissertation research project investigates the impacts of cross-border trade and exchange on diplomatic relations and on land and wildlife management. Investigators specifically examine the role that management of vertebrate wildlife has on cross-border trade and border management.  Research findings have translational impact on border security and workforce development in diplomacy and land administration.  

Research findings will contribute to the understanding of diplomatic and trade relations. In addition to training a graduate student, research findings will be disseminated to inform the development of land management and/or cross-border trade and diplomatic strength. Expansion of our understanding of the role that land and wildlife administration play in the governance of trade and diplomacy will contribute to NSF’s priorities of fueling economic prosperity, national security, and global competitiveness. It will also contribute to the science of national security, and secure borders.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

por.por_cntn:
This study deepens our understanding of diplomatic relations and their effects on the domestic life of host countries through a case study on elite falconry in Pakistan. Pakistan and the Gulf states, particularly Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates (UAE), and Qatar, share close socio-cultural, diplomatic, and economic relations. Pakistan provides security cooperation to its Gulf state allies and secures diplomatic and trade benefits in return. This project explores the role of elite falconry within these diplomatic relations and investigates how they shape sovereignty, domestic conservation laws, and the everyday lives of local communities. Termed a “heritage sport” in the Arab world, foreign elites with economic influence, political power, and prestige pursue Houbara bustards (locally called Taloor) into their wintering grounds in Pakistan. This research sheds light on the many ways that these relations shape domestic conservation laws to allow the hunting of the protected Taloor bird, and in so doing, disrupt local land uses and moral frameworks. 

Situated at the intersection of political, ecological, multispecies, and legal dynamics and theories, this project asks: “What are the social, political, discursive, and material dynamics surrounding elite falconry at local, national, and translational scales?” To answer this overarching question, the project asks the following specific questions: 

Q1: What are the political, economic and multispecies dynamics involved in the configuration of Pakistan’s diplomacy with the Gulf states of Saudi Arabia, the UAE, and Qatar? 

Q2: What effects do these diplomatic relations have on national and provincial wildlife laws, conservation practices, and territorial control, and how has Pakistani sovereignty been reconfigured in the process? 

Q3. How have these changes in laws and conservation practices influenced the lands, lives, and relationalities of native Sindhi farmers, herders, and the Taloor birds?

This 14-month project employed content analysis of grey literature and qualitative research methods (systematic observation, interviews) at multiple urban and rural “sites” (embassies, government offices, and rural communities of Sindh Province) to examine the political, legal, and material effects of elite falconry. 

In terms of intellectual merits, the project deepens our understanding of international diplomacy by exploring the role of non-human birds in Pakistan-Gulf state diplomacy and economic ties, such as the establishment of the Special Investment Facilitation Council (SIFC) that attracts investment from the Gulf states. Bringing into conversation ethnographic investigations and theoretical insights on increased engagement of animals in international politics, especially diplomatic realms, the project advances the concept of “multispecies diplomacy” in which the non-human birds, including Taloor and falcons, along with humans and state institutions, configure diplomatic and trade relations between Pakistan and the Gulf states. In so doing, the project engages in broader conversations surrounding the role of non-humans as entities that actively shape the world, yet takes this beyond the local level to reveal them as co-participants in international relations. 

The project also contributes to longstanding anthropological studies of host-guest relations, through an ethnographic exploration of Taloor as “winged guests”. In so doing, this project suggests ways to incorporate local norms of hospitality into the conservation and governance of migratory species crossing multiple political borders. The project supports scholarship in cultural anthropology by studying local relationships with land and wildlife and examining how these relations are influenced by elite falconry. This project also contributes to the anthropology of Pakistan and adds geographical breadth to broader anthropological literature on elite hunting sports, conservation practices, wildlife laws, and disadvantaged communities. The project contributes to ornithology by developing methodological insights into how qualitative methods can supplement ornithological data in sensitive areas where technical equipment such as camera traps could not be installed due to security concerns. 

In terms of broader impacts, NSF funding has contributed to the Co-PI's professional development and enabled substantial progress towards the timely completion of his PhD. Further impacts are expected for i. local communities and ii. conservation. To highlight the impacts of falconry on local lives, the CoPI presented (online) the project’s preliminary observations at the Symposium on Integrative Conservation (SIC) in 2025. He will also share a policy brief with the Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Pakistan (MoFA) in Fall 2027, suggesting how local perspectives might be integrated into foreign policy and plans to foster diplomacy while recognizing local rights to lands and ensuring their safety. For conservation, the Co-PI will publish two articles and a blog post in mainstream national and international media outlets in Spring 2028, highlighting how political, legal, and cultural dynamics shape conservation of threatened migratory Taloor birds. The articles will propose wildlife laws, policies, and practices that are culturally informed and grounded in local moralities and relationalities. The Co-PI will also host a multi-stakeholder dialogue in Karachi with the support of WWF and IUCN to share findings and foster dialogue around how best to integrate local perspectives on lands and livelihoods and balance Taloor conservation with local and national interests.
